stops.name: Florence, the first sentence in absentia
stops.campa: The podestà Cante de' Gabrielli da Gubbio convicts Dante in absence on charges of barratry, corruption, and opposition to the Pope and to Charles of Valois, fines him five thousand florins he cannot pay, and bars him from office for two years. Dante refuses to appear and answer, knowing an appearance is itself a confession under Black Guelph law. He will spend the rest of his years, in his own words, going as a pilgrim, almost a beggar, through nearly every province where this Italian tongue is spoken, showing against his will the wound that Fortune deals.
stops.quote: per le parti quasi tutte a le quali questa lingua si stende, peregrino, quasi mendicando, sono andato, mostrando contra mia voglia la piaga de la fortuna

stops.name: Florence, the second sentence: death by fire
stops.campa: A second decree, harsher than the first, condemns Dante and fourteen others by name to be burned alive should they ever fall into the power of the commune. His sons, once they come of age, will be named in a further decree of the same kind. From this day the sentence is never revoked in his lifetime; the city that made him a poet in her own tongue keeps a fire lit for him, in law, for the remaining nineteen years he has left to live.

stops.name: San Godenzo, the pact of the exiles
stops.campa: In the choir of the Benedictine abbey of San Godenzo, eighteen heads of the exiled White Guelphs and Ghibellines gather and swear a compact, notarized by Giovanni Buto d'Ampinana: to indemnify the Ubaldini counts of the Mugello for any damage the coming war of return does to their castles, in exchange for men and passage. Dante's name stands among the signers, the last time it will ever stand joined to a faction's cause. Within a few years he will break from these same allies and call their whole company wicked and foolish, a party of one from then on.

stops.name: Forlì, the muster under Scarpetta Ordelaffi
stops.campa: The exiled Whites and their Ghibelline allies gather an army under the Forlì captain Scarpetta Ordelaffi, hoping to fight their way back into Florence. Dante rides among them still, one voice in a council of the disaffected, though he already distrusts the enterprise. The war of return will end in ruinous defeat, at Puliciano in the Mugello and then under Florence's own walls at La Lastra; long before those fields are lost, Dante has begun to draw apart from the company whose folly he will soon condemn outright, in the words of an ancestor not yet spoken to him.

stops.name: Verona, the first refuge, Bartolomeo della Scala
stops.campa: Dante finds his first true shelter at the court of Bartolomeo della Scala, lord of Verona, whose house bears the ladder and the eagle on its crest. Here for the first time since Florence a great household feeds and houses him not as a mendicant but as an honored guest, though the bread is another man's bread and the stairs he climbs are another man's stairs. It is a hospitality he will still be praising, and still tasting the bitterness under, when his own ancestor foretells it to him from inside a sphere of fire twelve years hence.
stops.quote: Lo primo tuo refugio e 'l primo ostello sarà la cortesia del gran Lombardo che 'n su la scala porta il santo uccello.

stops.name: Bologna, the years of study and De Vulgari Eloquentia
stops.campa: Among the schools of Bologna, where he had studied as a young man before the exile, Dante now takes up two ambitious unfinished treatises: the Convivio, a banquet of philosophy set out in the vernacular for those shut out of Latin learning, and the De Vulgari Eloquentia, the first treatise ever written on what makes an Italian vernacular fit for the highest poetry. No one before him, he declares in its opening line, has ever treated the doctrine of eloquence in the vulgar tongue. He is still building, in exile, the very language his sentence was written in.
stops.quote: Cum neminem ante nos de vulgaris eloquentiae doctrina quicquam inveniamus tractasse...

stops.name: Lunigiana, the Malaspina court and the Peace of Castelnuovo
stops.campa: Taken in by the Malaspina marquises, Dante repays their courtesy in the coin he has: on this morning in the piazza of Castelnuovo Magra, Marquis Franceschino Malaspina names him executor, procurator, and special ambassador with full power to conclude, on the whole Ghibelline branch's behalf, a peace with Antonio Nuvolone da Camilla, bishop-count of Luni, ending a long and bitter feud over the Lunigiana valleys. The exile who cannot enter his own city as a private man signs a treaty between a marquis and a bishop as a plenipotentiary.

stops.name: Casentino, Poppi Castle and the canto of Ugolino
stops.campa: At Poppi, guest of Count Guido da Battifolle and his countess Gherardesca, Dante writes three Latin letters in her name to the Empress Margherita of Brabant. Gherardesca is the daughter of Count Ugolino della Gherardesca of Pisa, starved to death with his sons and grandsons in the Tower of Hunger for an alleged betrayal; inside these same castle walls, under this same roof, Dante composes the canto that gives Ugolino's ravenous ghost, gnawing the skull of the archbishop who caged him, its final and most terrible line.
stops.quote: Poscia, più che 'l dolor, poté 'l digiuno.

stops.name: Lucca, refuge and Gentucca
stops.campa: Somewhere among the cities of his wandering Dante passes months at Lucca, sheltered, tradition says, in the house of Gentucca Morla; the shade of the poet Bonagiunta Orbicciani will greet him in Purgatory itself with news of an unwed Lucchese woman who will yet make that city please him, and asks whether he is truly the one who drew forth the new rhymes beginning with the words about women who have understanding of love. Dante answers that he is only a scribe, taking down what Love itself dictates within him.
stops.quote: Ma dì s'i' veggio qui colui che fore trasse le nove rime, cominciando 'Donne ch'avete intelletto d'amore'.

stops.name: Verona, the court of Cangrande della Scala
stops.campa: Dante returns to Verona, now ruled by Bartolomeo's younger brother Cangrande, the Great Dog, imperial vicar, the most magnificent lord in Lombardy and the most generous host of Dante's whole exile. Here he is given not charity but honor, a household of his own within the household, years of settled work on the Paradiso. His ancestor Cacciaguida, still unspoken to him at this point of the story but already speaking of it from Mars, foretells that this young lord, born under a strong star, will do deeds his enemies will not be able to keep silent about, however they try.
stops.quote: Con lui vedrai colui che 'mpresso fue, nascendo, sì da questa stella forte, che notabili fier l'opere sue.

stops.name: Verona, the Epistle to Cangrande
stops.campa: In a long Latin letter of dedication, Dante gives his protector, and the ages after him, the only key to the Commedia's meaning that its own author will ever set down in plain prose: that the poem is polysemous, carrying more than one sense at once, literal and allegorical together, and that its whole aim, and the aim of every part of it, is to lead those living this present life out of the state of misery and into the state of felicity. He dedicates the Paradiso, canticle by canticle, to the lord under whose roof he writes it.
stops.quote: finis totius et partis est removere viventes in hac vita de statu miserie et perducere ad statum felicitatis
stops.quote_source: Epistola XIII, to Cangrande della Scala, §39 (authorship debated by some scholars)

stops.name: Verona, the Quaestio de aqua et terra
stops.campa: Before the assembled clergy and learned men of Verona, in the church of Sant'Elena beside the cathedral, Dante reads a formal scholastic disputation on a question much argued in the schools: whether water, anywhere on the globe, rises higher than the dry land, even at the antipodes. He answers no, and defends it point by point against the philosophers, the very same cosmography by which, in his poem, the mountain of Purgatory stands alone out of the southern ocean, the one dry land raised up on the far side of the world from Jerusalem.
